content: 1. Historical data indicate that microfilaricidal drugs, such as diethylcarbamazine citrate (DEC-C), can cause cutaneous and/or systemic reactions of varying severity, known as the Mazzotti reaction, as well as ophthalmological reactions in patients with onchocerciasis. These reactions are likely due to allergic and inflammatory responses triggered by the death of microfilariae. 2. Patients treated with STROMECTOL for onchocerciasis may experience these reactions in addition to adverse effects that may be possibly, probably, or definitively related to the drug itself. Severe Mazzotti reactions have not been studied in controlled clinical trials. Management of postural hypotension in such cases has included oral hydration, recumbency, intravenous normal saline, and/or parenteral corticosteroids. Antihistamines and/or aspirin have been used for mild to moderate cases. 3. Patients with hyperreactive onchodermatitis (sowda) may be more prone to severe adverse reactions, such as edema and worsening of onchodermatitis, following treatment with microfilaricidal drugs. 4. Rarely, patients with onchocerciasis who are heavily infected with Loa loa may develop serious or fatal encephalopathy, either spontaneously or after treatment with an effective microfilaricide. Reported symptoms in such cases include pain (e.g., neck and back pain), red eye, conjunctival hemorrhage, dyspnea, urinary and/or fecal incontinence, difficulty standing or walking, mental status changes, confusion, lethargy, stupor, seizures, or coma. This syndrome has been observed very rarely following ivermectin use. 5. For individuals requiring ivermectin treatment who have had significant exposure to Loa loa-endemic areas in West or Central Africa, pretreatment assessment for loiasis and careful post-treatment monitoring are recommended. 6. STROMECTOL should be taken on an empty stomach with water. For strongyloidiasis, patients should be reminded of the need for repeated stool examinations to confirm clearance of Strongyloides stercoralis infection. For onchocerciasis, patients should be informed that treatment with STROMECTOL does not kill adult Onchocerca parasites, necessitating repeated follow-up and retreatment. 7. Long-term animal studies to evaluate the carcinogenic potential of ivermectin have not been conducted. Ivermectin was not genotoxic in various in vitro assays, including the Ames microbial mutagenicity assay, mouse lymphoma cell line assays, and unscheduled DNA synthesis assays in human fibroblasts. Fertility in rats was not adversely affected at doses up to three times the maximum recommended human dose (on a mg/m²/day basis). 8. Teratogenic effects, such as cleft palate and clubbed forepaws (in rabbits), were observed in animal studies only at or near maternally toxic doses. Ivermectin does not appear to be selectively fetotoxic to the developing fetus. However, there are no adequate and well-controlled studies in pregnant women, and ivermectin should not be used during pregnancy as its safety has not been established. 9. STROMECTOL is excreted in low concentrations in human breast milk. Treatment of breastfeeding mothers should only be undertaken if the risk of delaying treatment to the mother outweighs the potential risk to the newborn. 10. The safety and effectiveness of ivermectin in pediatric patients weighing less than 15 kg have not been established. 11. Clinical studies of STROMECTOL did not include sufficient numbers of subjects aged 65 and older to determine whether they respond differently from younger patients. However, other clinical experience has not identified differences in responses between elderly and younger patients. Treatment of elderly patients should be cautious, considering the greater likelihood of decreased hepatic, renal, or cardiac function, as well as concomitant diseases or other drug therapies. 12. In immunocompromised patients, including those with HIV, being treated for intestinal strongyloidiasis, repeated courses of therapy may be required. Adequate and well-controlled clinical studies have not been conducted in such patients to determine the optimal dosing regimen. Monthly treatments may be helpful, but cure may not always be achievable.
